strengths: Strong and broad empirical evidence: SOTA results across vision classification (8/14/20 tasks on ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14), dense prediction (NYUv2), and NLP (GLUE), consistently approaching or matching individual-model upper bounds, with per-task results in the appendix.

A compelling and well-executed motivating study: the correlation between cross-task performance and merge quality (r=0.863, p<0.001 on 20 tasks) is a genuinely interesting observation, and the two-stage pilot protocol (Figure 3) cleanly demonstrates that adapting a single layer improves functional alignment.

Thoughtful analysis distinguishing the proposed self-labeling objective from entropy minimization: the Spearman correlation analysis (Figure 4, Table C) showing entropy's proxy correlation degrades during training while cross-entropy self-labeling stays high provides real justification for the design choice, going beyond 'it works better'.

Thorough ablations and analyses: component ablation (joint vs. single-component optimization), layer-choice study, coefficient initialization robustness, transferability of adapted layers to other merging methods (Table 4), corruption robustness, and sparsity visualization — collectively well beyond typical baselines-only evaluation.

Honest and substantive treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly acknowledges dependence on expert model quality, reports negative cases (SVHN in the pilot study), and discloses the sequential-update implementation detail with its effect on a baseline's performance.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full hyperparameters in Appendix A, public fine-tuned checkpoints used where possible, standard benchmarks, and a code release promise.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients — test-time learning of merging coefficients (AdaMerging), pseudo-labeling/self-distillation from expert models, and jointly adapting a task head — are each well-established; the method is a sensible recombination. The 'synergy' framing is largely narrative, as the objective (matching individual experts) does not explicitly optimize cross-task synergy.

The theoretical justification is thin and somewhat disconnected from the method: Proposition 1 is a direct application of Jensen's inequality under strong assumptions (cross-task linearity, convex output loss), and it argues that synergy helps merging in general — it neither explains why the proposed objective finds synergistic task vectors nor provides any guidance for the algorithm.

There is a gap between the motivation and the mechanism: the paper argues merging should 'actively enhance tasks,' but the method merely distills toward individual expert predictions on unlabeled test data; nothing in the objective encourages one task to improve another, so the claimed conceptual advance is only loosely instantiated.

Comparisons with test-time adaptive baselines may not be fully fair: the authors note their sequential-update strategy alone improves AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6, but it is unclear whether competing methods were given the same optimization-schedule advantage, so part of the reported margin may be attributable to an implementation trick rather than the core idea.

Like other test-time adaptive methods, the approach optimizes on the (unlabeled) test distribution, which complicates the meaning of the reported test accuracies relative to training-free methods; while corruption experiments partially address this, the setting deserves more explicit discussion of when such test-set access is legitimate.

The dependence of performance on merging-coefficient initialization settings differs across task counts (0.3 for 8 tasks, 0.1 for 14/20 tasks), introducing a mild hyperparameter sensitivity that is disclosed but not deeply analyzed, and the expert-quality ceiling is acknowledged but left unresolved.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three modalities: 8/14/20-task vision classification (ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14), dense prediction on NYUv2 (segmentation, depth, normals), and 8 GLUE tasks with RoBERTa — coverage that exceeds most merging papers
Consistently strong results, approaching individual-model upper bounds (e.g., 90.1 vs 90.5 on 8-task ViT-B/32) and large margins over prior test-time adaptive methods

Well-executed motivation studies: the correlation between cross-task performance and merge quality (r=0.863), the corruption robustness analysis, and the Spearman correlation analysis justifying the self-labeling objective over entropy minimization (Figure 4, Table C)

Thorough ablations: joint vs. individual component optimization (Table 5), layer-choice analysis (Figure 5, Table B), loss-function comparison (Figure C), initialization robustness (Figure 6b), sparsity analysis (Figures F/G), and transferability of adapted layers to other merging methods (Table 4)
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging dependence on expert-model quality and reporting negative cases (e.g., SVHN in the pilot study)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially AdaMerging with two modifications: (1) replacing entropy minimization with cross-entropy against pseudo-labels from the individual fine-tuned models (a classic self-labeling/distillation technique, Lee et al. 2013), and (2) additionally training the task-specific head. Both components are well-established; the contribution is their combination and empirical tuning rather than a new mechanism

The headline 'synergy' framing is overstated. Because the training signal is to mimic the individual expert models, the method's ceiling is the individual models' performance (acknowledged in Figure 6a and the limitations section). This is distillation toward the multi-task upper bound, not genuinely emergent cross-task synergy; the reframing of the field's goal from non-interference to synergy is asserted more than demonstrated

The theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) is close to trivial: it is Jensen's inequality applied under an assumed cross-task linearity and convexity, with a one-epsilon gap between two assumed cases. It provides little explanatory power for why the proposed optimization procedure works

Efficiency claims are undercut. Test-time adaptation requires storing and running all K fine-tuned expert models as teachers, plus per-task heads. The deployed cost is close to ensembling/individual models, weakening the core motivation of merging (a single model without the original task-specific artifacts)
Some comparisons appear incomplete: Table 2 (dense prediction) omits AdaMerging and WEMoE — the strongest adaptive baselines from Table 1 — leaving the fairness of the dense-prediction claims unclear

The central pilot-study evidence is correlational on a single backbone (ViT-B/32, 20 tasks); no causal intervention or cross-backbone validation of the cross-task-performance → merge-quality hypothesis is provided beyond the indirect layer ablations

Adaptation uses the unlabeled test set itself for optimization (500–1000 iterations of batch updates on test data), which raises standard test-set-contamination concerns; the paper's defense via TTA convention is plausible but deserves a more careful treatment, including evaluation on held-out shifted splits

Reproducibility is weakened by deferred code release ('upon publication'); no anonymous artifact is provided for verification of the sequential-update scheme, which the appendix itself admits gives a nontrivial free gain (80.1% → 81.6%) over the standard simultaneous-update protocol used by all baselines

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 8/14/20 vision classification tasks (ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14), dense prediction on NYUv2 (segmentation, depth, surface normals), and 8 GLUE NLP tasks with RoBERTa, with mean and std over 5 runs reported for the proposed method.

Well-motivated pilot study establishing a quantitative link between cross-task performance and merging quality (r = 0.863, p < 0.001), which provides genuine insight beyond prior non-interference-centric framing.

Careful diagnosis of why entropy minimization is unstable (Spearman correlation with ground-truth loss degrades after training, e.g., -1.49 on Cars), empirically justifying the self-labeling cross-entropy objective, with additional loss-function comparisons in the appendix.

Strong and consistent state-of-the-art results, including notable gains over test-time adaptive baselines (e.g., 90.1 vs 87.4 on 8-task ViT-B/32) and robustness under corrupted test data where both training-free and adaptive baselines degrade substantially.

Thorough ablations: joint vs. individual optimization of coefficients and task layer, choice of adapted layer (single-layer works, multi-layer fails), coefficient initialization sensitivity, transferability of adapted layers to other merging encoders (+10.5%p on TA), sparsity analysis, convergence, and per-task breakdowns.
Honest limitations section and reasonable reproducibility information (hardware, hyperparameters, promised code release); no ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is technically trivial: it follows directly from Jensen's inequality under the assumed cross-task linearity and convexity, and the assumptions are strong and unverified for the actual models used; the 'theoretical justification' largely repackages the motivating intuition.

Conceptual novelty is modest: the method is essentially test-time knowledge distillation from the individual fine-tuned experts (pseudo-labeling) combined with AdaMerging-style coefficient learning plus tuning of the task-specific layer; the framing of 'redefining the goal of model merging' oversells what is an incremental, though effective, combination of known ingredients.

Because the method distills expert predictions on the unlabeled test set, its near-individual performance raises a question of whether the 'merged' model is meaningfully a merged model versus a distillation artifact; this deserves more critical discussion, though the transferability analysis (Table 4) partially mitigates it.

Evaluation is limited to CLIP ViT and RoBERTa-base backbones with publicly available fine-tuned checkpoints; no experiments on larger or generative/LLM-scale merging, so scalability claims are bounded.

Some results are not uniformly dominant (e.g., QQP and MNLI lag behind EMR-Merging in Table 3; SVHN shows negative gains in the pilot study), and per-task reliability could be discussed more candidly.

Several key details (confidence-based filtering, sequential update strategy that itself improves AdaMerging from 80.1% to 81.6%) are deferred to the appendix, and their individual contributions relative to the core idea are not fully disentangled.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: 8/14/20-task vision merging on ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14, dense prediction on NYUv2, NLP on RoBERTa (GLUE) and FLAN-T5, with 5-run standard deviations, consistently outperforming a wide set of recent baselines (EMR-Merging, ISO-Merging, WEMoE, ProbSurgery, etc.).

Well-motivated pilot study: the correlation between cross-task performance and merge quality (r=0.863, p<0.001, Figure 2) and the two-stage alignment protocol (Figure 3) give the method a clear empirical rationale beyond pure engineering.

Extensive and informative analyses: ablations showing complementarity of coefficient + single-layer adaptation (Table 6), transferability of the adapted layer to other merged encoders (Table 4), positive/negative transfer accounting (Figure 5), robustness to corrupted/backdoored experts (Tables 7-8), efficiency (Table 9, Appendix E.6), data-scarcity/online TTA settings (Table C), and empirical verification of the cross-task linearity assumption (Table G).

The stress test merging models from different initializations (disjoint basins, Table 5) is a genuinely interesting result showing the method works where linear-mode-connectivity-based merging fundamentally fails.
Honest limitations section: dependence on expert quality, requirement for unlabeled target inputs, and acknowledged open questions about coefficient/layer interaction.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is modest: SyMerge is essentially AdaMerging-style coefficient tuning plus a single task-specific layer, supervised by expert predictions (self-labeling/distillation). This combines existing ideas (test-time merging from AdaMerging; feature/layer adaptation from Surgery) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The central 'synergy' claim is not convincingly demonstrated. Since the training signal is mimicry of the individual experts, the mechanism is better characterized as distillation-based knowledge recovery than as tasks 'actively improving one another.' On several NLP tasks (e.g., QQP 85.2 vs. 91.4, MNLI 84.0 vs. 87.2), the merged model remains below individual models, and the positive/negative transfer analysis (Figure 5) shows the merged model mostly preserves individual knowledge rather than exceeding it.

The theoretical support (Proposition 3.1) is a direct application of Jensen's inequality under an assumed cross-task linearity condition; it formalizes that positive cross-task transfer tightens an upper bound but offers limited insight into the actual optimization or the proposed method, which does not directly optimize cross-task performance.

The disjoint-basin result, while striking, is limited to a single two-task configuration (EuroSAT/DTD) with no analysis of why joint optimization bridges the loss barrier; the claim that this 'realigns conflicting representations' is asserted rather than analyzed.

Reliance on the individual expert models at test time (both for predictions and, implicitly, as a computational cost in sequential updates) is a stronger assumption than training-free merging and weakens the 'merging' framing; the paper is transparent about this, but it narrows the practical setting relative to what the narrative implies.

Minor presentation issues: abstract is truncated ('Our code is available a'), Figure 1 legend mixing training-free and test-time methods is confusing, and the dense-prediction and disjoint-basin studies involve small numbers of tasks, limiting generalizability of those conclusions.

strengths: Comprehensive and unusually broad empirical coverage: 8/14/20 vision tasks (ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14), dense prediction on NYUv2 (segmentation, depth, surface normals), 8 GLUE tasks with RoBERTa, and an FLAN-T5 extension, with extensive per-task results in the appendix.

The pilot study linking cross-task performance to merge quality (r = 0.863, Fig. 2) and the two-stage alignment protocol (Fig. 3) provide a clear, empirically grounded motivation, and the transferability check (Table 4) and encoder-quality ablation (Table D) support the claim that gains are not purely from head fine-tuning.

Thorough supporting analyses: loss-correlation analysis motivating self-labeling over entropy minimization, component ablations (Table 6), layer-choice ablations (Fig. 6, Table E), confidence-filtering ablation (Table H), robustness to corrupted/backdoored experts (Tables 7-8), data-scarcity and online TTA settings (Table C), and computational cost comparisons (Tables 9, I, J).

Limitations are discussed honestly (dependence on expert quality, need for unlabeled target inputs), and the code and reproducibility details (hyperparameters, sequential update protocol, baselines) are documented extensively in Appendix B.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty over AdaMerging: the core deltas are (i) jointly optimizing coefficients plus a single task-specific layer and (ii) replacing entropy minimization with expert-guided pseudo-labeling. Both are plausible but incremental refinements of existing test-time merging, and the paper frames them as a redefinition of the field's goal ('from non-interference to synergy'), which the evidence does not fully substantiate.

The method requires storing and running all K individually fine-tuned experts at test time to generate self-labels, which substantially weakens the practical motivation of merging (a single compact multi-task model without keeping the experts). While sequential inference and caching mitigate runtime, the storage/access assumption deserves a sharper discussion; a comparison against simply ensembling or majority-voting the experts is missing, which would clarify how much of the gain is distillation of an implicit ensemble rather than genuine 'synergy'.

The headline disjoint-basin result (Table 5, 96.2% on EuroSAT / 79.1% avg. from models with different initializations) is an extraordinary claim that a coefficient plus a single-layer adaptation can bridge a severe loss barrier between different CLIP checkpoints. The mechanism is not explained, and given that the self-labels come from the individual experts, it is not clear this is 'merging' at all rather than expert-conditioned adaptation. This result needs stronger analysis and corroboration.

The 'theoretical backup' (Prop. 3.1) is a trivial two-line application of Jensen's inequality under cross-task linearity, and it supports only that a convexity-tightened bound is lower in the synergistic case; it does not analyze the proposed method and adds little scientific value.

The synergy narrative is somewhat overclaimed: several key results (e.g., the pilot study) amount to retraining a task head on a merged encoder, a known and largely expected benefit; some tasks show limited or negative gains (SVHN in Fig. 3b), and per-task tables reveal scattered regressions (e.g., QQP, QNLI in Table 3) that are not analyzed.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends with a broken sentence ('Our code is available a'), the odd section title 'Theoretical Backup', apparent label overlap/corruption in Figure 1, and reliance on baseline numbers partially reproduced from prior works makes strict comparability (e.g., which baselines use the same unlabeled-data budget and update schedule) harder to verify. Reporting variance for their method only, across 5 runs, is also inconsistent with the baseline reporting.

The method's dependence on transductive multi-epoch optimization over the unlabeled test set (500 iterations, batch 32) is stronger than typical online TTA assumptions; the privacy/latency limitation is acknowledged but its implications for the claimed SOTA comparisons are not.

strengths: Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is validated across vision classification (8/14/20 tasks on ViT-B/32 and L/14), dense prediction (NYUv2 segmentation/depth/normals), NLP (GLUE on RoBERTa, plus FLAN-T5 generative setting), consistently outperforming a wide range of recent training-free and test-time merging baselines with reported std over 5 runs.

The motivation is well constructed: the pilot study relating cross-task performance to merge quality (r = 0.863) and the two-stage single-layer adaptation protocol provide an interpretable, empirically grounded rationale for the design, and the loss-correlation analysis (Fig. 4, Table F) carefully justifies expert-guided self-labeling over entropy minimization.

The paper is unusually thorough in its analyses: ablations on trainable components and layer choice, robustness to corrupted and backdoored experts, merging across disjoint basins, online/limited-data TTA regimes, computational cost, and coefficient sparsity. The ablation showing the merged encoder itself improves (Table D: 69.1 -> 82.4 with zero-shot heads) directly addresses the concern that gains come only from head adaptation.

Honest limitations section covering dependence on expert quality, need for unlabeled target inputs, and open questions; theoretical assumptions (cross-task linearity) are explicitly verified empirically (Table G).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: standard public checkpoints, detailed hyperparameters, batch sizes, iteration counts, and sequential-update protocol are documented, and code availability is stated.
weaknesses: The central 'synergy' claim is over-stated relative to the evidence. In most main tables SyMerge approaches but does not exceed the individual experts (e.g., 90.1 vs 90.5 on 8-task ViT-B/32; 83.9 vs 85.6 avg on GLUE), and the positive/negative transfer analysis (Fig. 5) is framed as best *preserving* individual knowledge. The objective is fundamentally expert distillation via pseudo-labels, which is closer to recovering expert performance than to tasks 'actively improving one another'. A clearer operational definition and direct evidence of genuine synergy (merged > expert on some tasks) would strengthen the framing.

Conceptual novelty is modest: the ingredients (task-vector coefficient tuning à la AdaMerging, single-layer/classifier adaptation à la Surgery/ProbSurgery, and pseudo-label distillation à la self-training) are all well established; the contribution is largely their combination plus the alignment analysis. The paper should sharpen what is new relative to Surgery/ProbSurgery beyond the joint coefficient optimization.

The theory (Proposition 3.1) is a direct Jensen's inequality argument under strong assumptions (exact cross-task linearity, output convexity) and mainly restates that a tighter bound yields a better model; it provides limited insight into when synergy will actually arise.

The pilot correlation study is conducted on a single setup (ViT-B/32, one benchmark family), and the disjoint-basin result uses only two tasks with a somewhat special configuration (no shared pre-trained checkpoint), so the generalization of these motivating results is not established.

Fairness/comparability concerns: the sequential per-task update strategy alone improves AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6, and confidence-based filtering adds gains; while the authors state settings are matched to baselines, the interaction of these implementation choices with reported improvements deserves more careful isolation against adapted baselines.

Test-time adaptation on the unlabeled test set itself (standard in TTA but relevant here since coefficients are tuned on test data) could raise questions about deployment realism; the online and limited-data experiments partially, but not fully, address this. There is also a minor presentation defect: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Our code is available a'), suggesting insufficient proofreading.
